persuade.name: Persuade
persuade.summary: Argument-driven keynote arc inspired by Ken Robinson: grip the audience, challenge the status quo, define the problem, anchor it in story and statistic, deliver a major revelation, propose change, and end on a question that stays with them.

beats.name: Gripping Introduction
beats.description: Open with a moment, image, or claim the audience can't easily look away from. The first sixty seconds buy you the next twenty minutes — spend them on something specific and emotionally charged, not on housekeeping.
beats.instructions: Draw in the audience with a compelling opener

beats.name: Challenge the Status Quo
beats.description: Call out the system, norm, or assumption that needs examination. Be precise about what you're disagreeing with so the rest of the talk can be specific in response. Avoid strawmen — name the strongest version of the view you're contesting.

beats.name: Present the Problem
beats.description: Define the issue the audience needs to care about. Concrete, scoped, attributable. The clearer the problem, the more credible the eventual solution.

beats.name: Personal Story
beats.description: Anchor the issue in a specific person, place, or moment. Story is what gets the argument past the audience's defenses. Pick a story that personalizes the data without overstating it.
beats.instructions: Share significant stories to illuminate the issue

beats.name: Statistic Shock
beats.description: Drop in a single statistic that recasts the scale of the problem. One number, presented well, lands harder than a dashboard. Cite the source so the audience can repeat it with confidence.
beats.instructions: Use impactful stats to highlight the gravity of the issue

beats.name: Historical Context
beats.description: Show how the issue evolved. Why it has the shape it does today, what was tried, what was missed. Historical context turns 'this is broken' into 'this stayed broken for these reasons.'
beats.instructions: Show the evolution or history of the issue

beats.name: Weave a Narrative
beats.description: Connect the threads — story, statistic, history — into a single argument. The audience should feel the case clicking together. This is the slide where rhetoric becomes architecture.

beats.name: Major Revelation
beats.description: Deliver the surprising or significant turn. The fact, finding, or reframing the rest of the talk has been earning. The revelation should redirect, not merely confirm.
beats.instructions: Deliver a surprising or significant discovery

beats.name: Propose Solution
beats.description: Advocate for the change you want. Concrete enough to be acted on, broad enough to inspire. Pair the solution with the smallest credible first step.
beats.instructions: Advocate for change or propose an actionable solution

beats.name: Final Question
beats.description: Close on a question rather than a summary. The right closing question follows the audience out of the room and into their conversations afterward.
beats.instructions: Finish with a thought-provoking question to stimulate audience thinking

executive.name: Executive
executive.summary: C-suite and senior leadership focused on strategic decisions, ROI, and big-picture outcomes. Highly time-constrained.
executive.description: C-suite and senior leaders deciding on strategy, ROI, and big-picture outcomes with very little time. Lead with the conclusion and keep to one insight per slide; set the key numbers in bold type and use as few bullet points as possible. Keep chart density low and the deck to 10-15 slides at most.

marketing.name: Marketing
marketing.summary: Marketing professionals analyzing campaign performance, brand metrics, and growth strategies.
marketing.description: Marketing professionals reviewing campaign performance, brand metrics, and growth strategy. Make the funnel visible, highlight engagement metrics, keep the brand consistent, and tell the story visually. Moderate chart density; 15-30 slides.

persuade.name: Persuade
persuade.summary: Change belief or win support for a specific argument, idea, or recommendation.
persuade.description: Use when the audience may be skeptical or undecided. Build a crisp thesis, support it with evidence, address objections, and end with a clear action.
persuade.outcome: The audience accepts the argument or supports the recommendation.

casual.name: Casual
casual.summary: Warm, plain-spoken voice for internal updates and customer storytelling.
casual.description: Friendly and direct. Use first- and second-person freely; favor short sentences and contractions. Numbers are still welcome — they just sit alongside human-scale framing rather than leading.
voiceCues: Favor short sentences and active voice.
Frame metrics with a human-scale anchor when possible.
samplePhrases: We shipped the new dashboard last week, and customers are already moving over.
Here's where we ended up on hiring this quarter.
It's been a busy month — here's the recap.

classic.name: Classic
classic.description: A timeless, clean, and versatile theme with balanced color contrasts and classic typography. Ideal for professional, readable presentations.

golden-yellow.name: Golden Yellow
golden-yellow.summary: Bright yellow and teal accents for optimistic, high-visibility decks.
golden-yellow.description: A warm yellow palette balanced by teal and navy. It is expressive, optimistic, and useful for bright public-facing stories.

cool-horizon.name: Cool Horizon
cool-horizon.summary: Cool blue-green palette tuned for professional business decks.
cool-horizon.description: A balanced cool-toned scheme with deep navy, business blues, and teal accents. It works well across strategy, finance, and technical narratives.

impact.name: Impact
impact.description: Impact is a sans serif OPF font scheme for Latin presentations, using Impact for headings with Grandview for body text.

tenorite.name: Tenorite
tenorite.description: Tenorite is a sans serif OPF font scheme for Latin presentations, using Tenorite Display for headings with Tenorite for body text.

cover.name: Cover
cover.summary: The opening slide: title, subtitle and an optional picture.
cover.description: Open a presentation with its subject and a short introduction. Add a picture when it helps establish the context.

text.name: Text
text.summary: Prose. Several blocks sit side by side when short and stack when long.
text.description: Explain one idea in continuous prose. Use paragraphs or flowing blocks for detail that needs to be read in sequence.

chart.name: Chart
chart.summary: One to six charts, with an optional note.
chart.description: Give a chart enough space to show its evidence. Use the title to state the conclusion and labels to explain the measures.

table-beside.name: Table beside
table-beside.summary: A table with commentary beside it.
table-beside.description: Place a table beside its interpretation. Use the supporting text to explain the conclusion without repeating every cell.

timeline.name: Timeline
timeline.summary: Dated events or a roadmap along one axis, with optional notes.
timeline.description: Show events or milestones in chronological order. Label each item with a date or stage and a concise description.

list.name: List
list.summary: Bulleted or numbered points; one long list flows into columns.
list.description: Present several related points in a clear sequence. Use bullets for independent points or numbered items for an ordered list.
